newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed oozes confidence, weighs up future.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed oozes confidence, weighs up future.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, self-avowed black sheep of Russian politics, has eased his way back effortlessly into civilian life after being ignominiously fired by President Boris Yeltsin for failing to toe the Kremlin line.
But the former paratroop commander, his confidence apparently undimmed by his sudden dismissal after just four months at the top, shows no signs of wanting to quit the limelight.

"Russia is the richest country in the world yet Russians are among the poorest people in the world. This cannot be right," Lebed boomed in his trademark bass voice on Friday, invoking the inequalities that could help him rebuild his political career.

Yeltsin signed the decree sacking Lebed as his security chief on Thursday in an act of high drama captured by the television cameras. The ailing president accused Lebed of naked ambition for the top job and a lack of team spirit.
But on Friday, his wife on his arm, the soldier-politician emerged from a Moscow theatre with the look of a conquering hero rather than a publicly humiliated official just out of a job.
"I shall take a rest, then I shall start to work," he told reporters with a broad smile, but gave no details.
"The Death of Ivan the Terrible", the play the Lebeds had just seen, carried rich parallels with contemporary Russian politics that journalists and theatre-goers were quick to draw.

The play, set in 16th century Moscow, depicts a world of cloak-and-dagger intrigue at the court of the dying Tsar Ivan -- a ruler renowned for his cruelty and ruthlessness -- as ambitious noblemen jostle for position.
"The situation in the country is exactly the same (as it was then)," Lebed said.
Asked whether he had learned anything from the tale of Ivan's gloomy, chaotic last days of power, he joked: "I've learned how not to run a country."

His vigorous manner contrasted with his former boss's haggard look in recent television appearances. Yeltsin, 65, is resting at a sanitorium outside Moscow ahead of heart surgery expected to take place next month.

Lebed has declined to criticise Yeltsin's decision to fire him, saying it would be impolite to speak ill of the sick but making clear he believed that Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and other rivals engineered his dismissal.
"I was a black sheep in the herd. It was only a matter of time before they sacked me. I am not part of their herd," he told a news conference on Thursday.
But nobody is hurrying to write off Lebed as a spent force.

"Alexander Lebed has beaten the record for the shortest spell in power...but he is also the only state official who has managed to accomplish, in a very short time, the task that was set for him," said the liberal daily Izvestia on Saturday.
The paper was referring to the peace accord negotiated by Lebed with separatists in breakaway Chechnya that was signed on August 31, putting an end to 21 months of bloody fighting there.
Punning on Lebed's name, which means swan, Izvestia added: "The swan's flight has been interrupted but not completed."

Lebed, who has denied charges by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov that he was preparing a "creeping coup", urged his supporters to remain calm after his sacking but predicted that Russia was in for a "hot autumn".
He cited discontent in the crumbling army and the future of the Chechnya peace process he sponsored as Yeltsin's envoy to the rebel region.
If fighting erupts again, Lebed is sure to say he alone in Moscow was responsible for establishing peace and blame the collapse of the ceasefire on the policies of his Kremlin rivals.
Such comments would be likely to boost his standing with ordinary Russians, most of whom are weary of the conflict.
Lebed won the support of 11 million people during the first round of presidential elections in June and a recent opinion poll found him to be the country's most trusted politician.

Before his sacking Lebed clashed with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who on Friday strengthened his hand when Yeltsin sacked armed forces chief of staff Mikhail Kolesnikov in what appeared to be part of a purge of the ministry's old guard.

Rodionov was quick to support Lebed's sacking and many members of the lower house of parliament, which met on Friday to discuss the political fallout from Lebed's dismissal, joined the establishment's vigorous criticism of the general.
